final.title: Rollback plans are not the main control
final.body:
Rollback plans sound tidy until you look at the actual workflow risk. In a small business, the real question is not “can we undo it later?” It is “what stops a mistake from moving forward while this automation runs?” If the wrong customer reply goes out, a duplicate invoice is created, or a manual step gets skipped, rolling back afterwards does not erase the damage already in motion.

That is why rollback is not enough on its own. It protects the previous state. It does not stop bad data, bad answers, or bad decisions from spreading through the process. For an owner, the better question is simple: which part of this workflow needs a gate before anything is committed?

Start with one repeatable process you are thinking about automating. Write down the three most damaging failure modes: wrong data, missed items, and duplicates. Then pick one human approval step that would block the worst one before it reaches payment, the inbox, or the CRM. If you are testing invoice extraction, spot-check a few entries against the source documents before anything is posted. That is a control. A rollback plan is still useful, but it is the backup plan, not the main defense.

Bareni’s policy is to keep accounts in the customer’s name and hand over finished code. That is no-lock-in positioning, not a warranty. The practical move is still the same: control the workflow first, then decide whether automation belongs there at all.
